newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's Milosevic shelves debate on labour laws.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's Milosevic shelves debate on labour laws.

text.p: Serbia's government, facing a tidal wave of street protests, said it was dropping debate of deeply unpopular labour laws which economists say could have made up to 800,000 people unemployed from January 1.

Serbia's President Slobodan Milosevic looked increasingly isolated on Tuesday in a crisis over disputed elections after sharp international criticism, plans to widen mass protests, and growing pressure from trade unions.

The independent Nezavisnost union said it would go ahead with a planned protest outside the opening of the Serbian parliament on Tuesday despite a sudden decision on Monday night to drop from the agenda discussion of the laws which were supposed to take effect from the start of January.

"The Serbian government has decided to withdraw from procedure the draft law on amendments to the law on labour relations owing to large number of proposed amendments and the need for further consultations," Tanjug news agency said.

Economists were unsure precisely where the postponement left the draft laws, which were intended to abolish a compulsory leave system under which workers were supposed to receive 60 percent of their wages during lay-offs.
Most of Serbia's state-controlled industry has still not recovered from being idled by 3-1/2 years of international sanctions, and many workers do little or nothing while at their posts.
In recent days there had been growing signs that the union movement was becoming more vocal about its grievances.

The usually pro-government Alliance of Independent Trade Unions of Yugoslavia broke new ground by backing Nezavisnost's decision last week to join the protests, although it stopped short of calling on its own members to take to the streets.

Up until Monday the alliance, Serbia's biggest trade union grouping, had held back from the conflict fearing specific grievances about pay and workers' rights and conditions could be submerged by the opposition's political agenda.

Nezavisnost, which became the first trade union to march publicly last week, said its protest outside parliament would go ahead on Tuesday despite the government's decision to shelve debate on new labour laws, citing a need for more consultation.
"This was probably a tactic by the government to defuse the situation in the hope that Nezavisnost would call off its action," one political commentator said.

Entering the 30th straight day of demonstrations against Milosevic's refusal to reinstate the results of annulled local election last month, Zajedno leader Vuk Draskovic said on Monday that opposition support was rock solid.

The opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition unveiled plans for marches from 30 separate towns to descend on Belgrade for New Year rallies, saying on Monday: "We will be world champions in protest marathons."

Security forces have kept a low profile policing the protests, which have taken on a carnival atmosphere, but the memory of 1991, when Milosevic used tanks to drive protesters from the streets, is still fresh.

On Monday students, workers and Zajedno supporters once more flocked to the daily rallies in Belgrade, but the crowd size fell short of the record 250,000 at the weekend. There were also protests in about 20 other Serbian towns.
Washington signalled its growing displeasure with Milosevic on Monday night when U.S. envoy John Kornblum urged the veteran Balkan leader to "yield to democratic pressures".

Milosevic took another blow in the tense face-off with the opposition on Monday after a court in the town of Smederevska Palanka ordered the local electoral commission to recognise the opposition victory in the November elections.
There was a similar ruling in the town of Nis on Sunday.
